behavioral.name: Behavioral
behavioral.interviewer_guidance: Probe for structure (situation, task, action, result), for the candidate's OWN contribution (I versus we), and for concrete, measurable outcomes. If the story stays general, ask for the specific moment, decision, or number.

coding.name: Coding
coding.interviewer_guidance: The candidate first explains an approach, then writes code in an editor; submitted code arrives as a fenced code block in their message. Never reveal the solution or write code for them. Give a small hint only if they are clearly stuck or ask for one. Probe: brute force versus optimal, time and space complexity, edge cases, tracing the problem's own example through their code, and any bug you can see in the submitted code. Keep probing until they have submitted working code and stated its complexity. The candidate may code in ANY language they choose; accept it as-is. Never ask them to switch or translate to another language.

system-design.name: System design
system-design.interviewer_guidance: Let the candidate lead, and let them drive the requirements. Probe in the natural order of a real design interview: functional and non-functional requirements, core entities and API, the high-level design, then deep dives on scaling, the data model, consistency, failure modes, and the tradeoffs behind each choice. Push harder on deep dives and tradeoffs for senior candidates.

behavioral.name: Behavioral
behavioral.description: A first-round screen: introduce yourself, walk through a project, why this company, and a behavioral question drawn from what the job emphasizes.
behavioral.question_guidance: A first-round behavioral screen, the kind run by a recruiter or hiring manager. Write these four questions, in this order, all of question type "behavioral": (1) an opener asking the candidate to introduce themselves and walk through their background, framed around this role; (2) a request to walk through a project they are proud of, steered toward the kind of work, domain, or stack this job involves; (3) why they want to work at this company and in this role specifically; (4) one behavioral 'tell me about a time' question targeting a responsibility or value the job description emphasizes (for example ownership, working through ambiguity, cross-team collaboration, mentoring, or shipping under deadlines).
behavioral.interviewer_guidance: A first-round behavioral screen, the kind run by a recruiter or hiring manager. Be warm and conversational, like a real screen. On 'why this company', probe whether the candidate actually knows what the company does and how the role fits their goals.

coding.name: Coding
coding.description: A technical coding round: two leetcode-style problems. Talk through your approach, write the code in the editor, and discuss complexity.
coding.question_guidance: A technical coding round with leetcode-style data-structure and algorithm problems, all of question type "coding". Write the problems so the first is easier than the second, calibrated to the candidate's level (entry: easy then easy-to-medium; mid: medium; senior: medium then medium-to-hard). The problems must exercise different core data structures or algorithmic techniques from each other. Choose each technique deliberately, across the full breadth of a typical coding interview, and prefer a less obvious technique over the first one the company's domain suggests. Where it fits naturally, dress a problem in the company's domain, but keep it a standard, well-defined algorithm problem solvable in about 20 minutes. Each question's text is the task alone, in plain text (no markdown headings): what the function must do, self-contained. Do NOT write the signature, the constraints, or examples in the text: give them in the question's signature, constraints and examples fields instead (they are shown to the candidate after the text), with exactly two examples, each small enough to work out by hand. Problems are LANGUAGE-AGNOSTIC: the candidate codes in whatever language they choose, regardless of the company's tech stack. Never name, require, or suggest a programming language, and never write the signature in one language's syntax; give it neutrally, as functionName(paramName: plain-English description of its type) -> plain-English description of the return type. Likewise describe the approaches in each brief in prose, not in a specific language.
coding.interviewer_guidance: A technical coding round on leetcode-style problems, run the way an engineer at this company would run it. The candidate codes in any language they choose, even if the company's tech stack or the problem's wording uses another one.

system-design.name: System design
system-design.description: A system-design round: one open-ended design problem drawn from the company's product. Drive requirements, a high-level design, and the deep dives.
system-design.question_guidance: A system-design round with exactly one design problem, of question type "system-design". Draw the problem from the company's actual product or domain (for a payments company, design a payment ledger; for a video company, design video upload and playback), sized to the candidate's level. State it at a high level in one to three sentences. The candidate is expected to drive the requirements, so do not list them.
system-design.interviewer_guidance: A system-design round on one open-ended design problem drawn from the company's product or domain, run the way an engineer at this company would run it.
